patient.chief_complaint: Progressive proximal leg weakness 6 months after completing SCLC chemotherapy
patient.history_present_illness: A 68-year-old woman with recently completed treatment for limited-stage small cell lung cancer presented with 3 months of progressive proximal leg weakness. She completed 4 cycles of carboplatin/etoposide chemotherapy with concurrent thoracic radiation 6 months ago and achieved a complete radiographic response. At her most recent surveillance visit, she reported difficulty rising from chairs — she now requires using both arm rests to push herself to standing — and difficulty climbing stairs. She initially attributed this to deconditioning after cancer treatment. Her oncologist referred her to rehabilitation, which helped minimally. She has also noted intermittent double vision when driving and reading, occurring in the afternoons but not in the mornings. She mentioned her mouth seems dry most of the time. Over the past 3 months, she has had mild difficulty chewing and her voice becomes nasal in the evenings. She denies sensory symptoms in her hands but has mild numbness in her feet (known carboplatin neuropathy). She denies dysphagia, ptosis in the morning, or respiratory symptoms. Her oncologist ordered a brain MRI and PET-CT which showed no cancer recurrence. She was referred to neurology with the working diagnosis of either carboplatin peripheral neuropathy or paraneoplastic syndrome from SCLC.

specialized_test.test_type: EMG, NCS, and Repetitive Nerve Stimulation

findings.significance: Reduced baseline CMAP in lower extremity — suggestive of pre-synaptic disorder
Reduced baseline CMAP — pre-synaptic NMJ disorder vs platinum neuropathy

findings.result: Baseline 0.9 mV increases to 2.2 mV after 10-second MVC

specialized_test.impression: Low baseline CMAP amplitudes (deltoid 0.9 mV; reference >3 mV) with 118% CMAP increment on 50 Hz repetitive nerve stimulation, exceeding the >100% threshold. Post-exercise facilitation demonstrated (baseline 0.9 mV increasing to 2.2 mV after brief maximum voluntary contraction). No pathological low-frequency decremental response. Superimposed axonal sensory neuropathy on sensory NCS. The electrophysiological findings indicate a pre-synaptic disorder of neuromuscular transmission consistent with Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. Clinical correlation and serological evaluation recommended.
recommended_actions: Correlation with neuromuscular antibody studies recommended.
Further clinical and imaging evaluation as directed.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS), paraneoplastic, secondary to SCLC recurrence (anti-VGCC positive, anti-SOX1 positive)

differential.key_features: Anti-AChR negative; low baseline CMAP not seen in MG; >100% increment at 50 Hz confirms LEMS; proximal leg weakness > ocular (typical LEMS distribution)
Axonal sensory neuropathy from carboplatin confirmed but cannot explain low CMAP with 118% facilitation or proximal motor weakness
Anti-Hu negative; NCS pattern is pre-synaptic NMJ not demyelinating neuropathy; VGCC antibodies confirm LEMS

optimal_actions.action: Perform RNS including high-rate (50 Hz) when low baseline CMAP identified
optimal_actions.expected_finding: 118% increment at 50 Hz — pathognomonic for LEMS; post-exercise facilitation
VGCC 0.48 nmol/L elevated; anti-SOX1 positive — SCLC recurrence concern

optimal_actions.action: PET-CT for SCLC recurrence (standard CT insufficient)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hypermetabolic paratracheal node 1.2 cm SUV 6.8 — SCLC recurrence

optimal_actions.action: Initiate amifampridine for symptomatic LEMS control while oncology manages SCLC

critical_actions: High-rate RNS (50 Hz) is diagnostic — >100% CMAP increment is pathognomonic for LEMS
PET-CT for SCLC recurrence — standard CT misses small recurrence
SCLC treatment is primary therapy — LEMS often dramatically improves with cancer control
Amifampridine (FDA-approved for LEMS) initiated for symptomatic relief
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT diagnose MG without performing high-rate RNS in patients with low baseline CMAP
Do NOT use standard CT alone to exclude SCLC recurrence in LEMS — PET-CT required
Do NOT treat as simple carboplatin neuropathy — LEMS is the primary NMJ diagnosis
key_reasoning_points: Low baseline CMAP amplitude is the key differentiator of LEMS from MG — in MG, baseline CMAP is normal
Greater than 100% CMAP increment at 50 Hz is pathognomonic for LEMS (pre-synaptic calcium accumulation enables transient NMJ improvement)
Anti-VGCC antibodies confirm the diagnosis; anti-SOX1 positive predicts SCLC etiology
SCLC treatment is the definitive treatment for paraneoplastic LEMS — amifampridine provides symptomatic relief
PET-CT detects SCLC recurrences invisible on standard CT — mandatory in anti-SOX1 positive LEMS

red_herrings.data_point: Prior completed SCLC treatment with 'complete response'
red_herrings.intended_effect: Clinician assumes SCLC is cured and attributes weakness to carboplatin neuropathy or deconditioning, not pursuing LEMS/SCLC recurrence workup
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: LEMS onset after apparently complete SCLC remission is a classic presentation of occult SCLC recurrence; anti-SOX1 positive and anti-VGCC confirm LEMS-SCLC; PET-CT reveals recurrence
